summary: B is the safer merge because it implements the requested convenience API without changing global request-body and Files.Add semantics. Neither patch fully satisfies the contract, but A’s explicit retry refactor is materially out of scope and prohibited.
reasons: B preserves FilesService.Add behavior, while A changes RawClient.Do so seekable bodies retry, gain Content-Length, and are no longer closed by the transport—contrary to the contract’s instruction to preserve Add and avoid retry refactors.
Both implementations incorrectly duplicate Add’s option handling, request construction, decoding, and missing-data error instead of routing through s.Add(ctx, body, contentType, opts...).
Both correctly use multipartbody.NewFile with field "file", validate inputs in implementation, and produce a buffered multipart body that can be replayed on retry.
A has stronger multipart and validation coverage, but that advantage does not outweigh its broad behavioral changes to all seekable RawClient request bodies.
risks_a: Violates scope and frozen behavior by altering shared RawClient retry and body-ownership semantics.
The generalized seek-and-reuse mechanism shares one mutable ReadSeeker across attempts and introduces new machinery where the established multipart helper was sufficient.
Upload still bypasses FilesService.Add, and no source-reader failure test is included.
risks_b: Upload bypasses FilesService.Add and duplicates its internals, risking future semantic drift.
Tests omit required validation and source-reader failure cases.
The retry test uses strings.NewReader rather than a genuinely non-replayable source stream, so it does not directly prove streamed input becomes replayable after encoding.
